name: Cognition
intro: Cognition, the company behind Devin and the Windsurf acquisition, grew its run rate roughly 13x in twelve months — from under $70M in late 2025 to nearly $900M by September 2026, when it raised $2B at a $48B valuation. Every publicly reported revenue, funding and valuation number is collected below, each traced back to a source.

modelTitle: How Devin Seats and Agent Usage Bill Together.
modelParagraphs: Cognition monetizes Devin and the Windsurf IDE through seat subscriptions and usage-based agent billing. Devin's autonomous, long-running tasks consume large amounts of model compute, so heavy users pay beyond their base plan — which is also why the company stays loss-making: its own compute bill is the primary cost driver.

The Windsurf acquisition added a conventional per-seat IDE business and enterprise distribution. Investors in the September 2026 round cited this combination — autonomous agents plus an incumbent-style developer footprint — as the reason AI coding is not being treated as a winner-take-all market against Cursor, GitHub Copilot and Claude Code.

faqs.a: Cognition's run-rate revenue reached roughly $900 million by September 2026, up from $492 million in May 2026 and under $70 million a year earlier — about 13x growth in twelve months. That implies around $75 million of monthly recurring revenue.
A $2 billion Series E in September 2026 valued Cognition at $48 billion, nearly double the $26 billion post-money valuation from its $1 billion raise just four months earlier, in May 2026.
No. Despite the revenue ramp, reporting around the September 2026 round describes the company as still operating at a loss, with model compute for Devin's autonomous tasks the primary cost driver.

faqs.q: How Did the Windsurf Acquisition Change Cognition's Business?
faqs.a: In July 2025, after OpenAI's bid for Windsurf collapsed, Cognition bought Windsurf's IDE business. That added a per-seat editor with an enterprise customer base on top of Devin, giving Cognition both an agent product and an incumbent-style distribution channel.

Devin is sold on seat subscriptions with usage-based billing beyond the included quota, since autonomous tasks consume variable amounts of compute. The Windsurf side is conventional per-seat editor pricing. Enterprise agreements layer seat administration and security requirements on top.
